D-Wave Quantum (QBTS) now sells whole quantum computers, not just computing time over the cloud, and those sales may be what its bulls are betting on. Yet revenue over the last twelve months fell 44.2% from a year earlier. The drop came from a single quarter: March-quarter revenue fell 80.9%, while June-quarter revenue was essentially flat. A year earlier, that March quarter included $12.6 million of revenue from D-Wave's first sale of an annealing system. The stock has also lost 63.9% over the past year, while the S&P 500 gained 13.3%. That is the contradiction: the company is selling whole machines, yet its revenue and its share price have both fallen. So how big are these computer sales next to the rest of D-Wave's business?

D-Wave Sold One Computer For Over A Year's Revenue

D-Wave sold an annealing quantum computer system to Florida Atlantic University for $20 million. That single deal exceeds the $12.4 million of revenue D-Wave reported over the twelve months ended June 30, 2026. Management prices these machines at $20 million to $40 million each, aiming the lower end at research labs and universities.

Most of that sale is still to come as revenue. During the June quarter, D-Wave reported about $300,000 in systems and other revenue, mainly from installation and site work for the Florida Atlantic machine, against $1.9 million from cloud subscriptions. Professional services added about $900,000.

Management maintains that D-Wave's annealing systems are currently the only quantum platforms executing production commercial workloads, while competitors continue to test enterprise applications on gate-model architectures. On the fiscal Q2 2026 call, management said every other system in the industry is still in research, and that it does not expect significant cloud revenue from D-Wave's own gate-model systems until around 2032. The rival systems management described all use the gate-model design, and D-Wave is developing gate-model machines alongside its annealing ones.

How Much Revenue Has D-Wave Already Signed?

D-Wave's backlog of signed contracts still to deliver was $40.7 million at June 30, 2026, up from $5.3 million a year earlier. Management expects about 57% of that backlog to become revenue within the next 12 months. That comes to about $23 million, nearly twice the revenue D-Wave reported over the last twelve months.

Management expects to ship two annealing systems over the rest of 2026, both likely in the fourth quarter, and it expects fourth-quarter revenue to make up the majority of the year's total. The Florida Atlantic machine is one of those two systems, and management expects some revenue from installing the machines in 2027.

title: Can Accenture Stock Rise 30% From Here?

Can Accenture Stock Rise 30% From Here?

Accenture (ACN) stock trades at 17.8 times earnings, compared to 22.8 for the median S&P 500 company, despite a 35.9% gain since September 30, 2026. A 30% rise from here depends on whether that discount marks a sound business on sale or a fair price for slower growth. A rise of that size is not new for the stock. It has climbed 30% or more within the year in 7 of the last 10 calendar years. So what does an investor get for 17.8 times earnings?

Accenture Grows Revenue And Returns Cash To Shareholders

An investor gets a growing, cash-rich business. Accenture sells consulting and managed services to enterprises and governments. Its revenue grew 6.5% to $74.2 billion in fiscal 2026. The operating margin was 15.8%, placing it just below the 15.9% peak for the twelve months to fiscal Q3 2018, the highest of any twelve-month period since fiscal 2017.

That profit turns into cash. Free cash flow was $11.6 billion in fiscal 2026, and management said Accenture returned a record $11.5 billion to shareholders. Debt rose to $13.4 billion at August 31, 2026, from $8.18 billion a year earlier, but $12.8 billion of cash nearly matched it. Yet the stock returned about 1% over the twelve months to October 29, 2026, compared to 13.3% for the S&P 500, with October's gain included.

How Fast Is Accenture Growing On Its Own?

Management said Accenture grew about 3% in fiscal 2026 without acquisitions, against 5% in local currency with its purchases counted. The company spent $4.9 billion on 17 acquisitions that year. Reported revenue growth was far faster a few years ago, at 21.9% in fiscal 2022. It fell to 1.2% in fiscal 2024 and rose to 7.4% in fiscal 2025. Reported growth of 6.5% in fiscal 2026 beat the 5.0% average of fiscal 2024 to 2026, but it is nowhere near the old pace.

Accenture also faces pressure on prices. Management said pricing was stable across fiscal 2026 but came in lower in many areas of the business in the fourth quarter. Management also said Accenture is giving clients more AI efficiencies and more than offsetting them with new work. That is the case for the discount: the price appears to assume that AI will cut what clients pay for the same work faster than Accenture can win new work.

Accenture Is Betting On AI Work And Acquisitions

Accenture's response is to build AI work and keep buying growth. It now has nearly 110,000 AI and data professionals, beyond its goal of 80,000 by the end of fiscal 2026. Management said Accenture's revenue from work with its 8 emerging AI and data partners more than doubled from fiscal 2025.

title: What Could Lift IBM Stock?
detail:
What Could Lift IBM Stock?

International Business Machines (IBM) stock returned 17.4% from September 30 to October 29, 2026, against 1.0% for the S&P 500. Even with that gain, holders are down 15.2% over the year to October 29. The company's profits also fluctuate, with a net margin of 28.4% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and 12.8% in the third quarter of 2026. So what would have to go right in IBM's business for the shares to keep climbing?

All Of IBM's Upside Comes From Selling More

IBM would have to keep selling more, because higher revenue accounts for all of the gain in a Trefis scenario built on the company's own figures. This scenario is arithmetic, not a forecast, and it assumes revenue growth of 8.5% a year for three years. That is 1.25 times the pace IBM delivered over the twelve months to September 2026. Under these assumptions, IBM shares would be worth about 18.8% more in three years, before dividends.

Revenue growth delivers the whole gain and then some, because the lower net margin in the scenario takes part of it back and the P/E stays where it is today. IBM drew most of its recent growth from software, its largest segment. In fiscal 2025, software provided $2.9 billion of the $4.7 billion increase in IBM's overall revenue.

When one segment supplies most of the growth, the company's pace rides on it. A recent example: 98% of Tesla's deliveries last quarter were a Model 3 or Model Y, and its deliveries fell two years in a row. Read Trefis Big Story: How Tesla Blundered.

Where Is IBM's Sales Growth Coming From Now?

Management said on the October 21 call that software still leads, with software revenue up 9% at constant currency in the third quarter of 2026. The finance chief added that the 9% included over four points of organic growth, with the rest from acquired businesses such as Confluent. Within the software business, Red Hat grew 11%, and OpenShift reached $2.4 billion of annual recurring revenue. In infrastructure, management said the z17 mainframe brought in more than $1 billion of extra revenue over six quarters compared with earlier programs.

IBM's total sales are not growing at the scenario's pace yet. Reported revenue rose 4.7% in the third quarter of 2026 from a year earlier. Management's guide of 4% to 5% for 2026 covers a year already reported through September, so most of that forecast consists of results already in. Management also said it does not expect the double-digit growth in transaction processing, its mainframe software, to keep going.

Investors eyeing Accenture (ACN) probably fear that AI allows clients to complete the same work with fewer consultants. Management says the new business AI generates outweighs what Accenture loses to AI efficiencies. The stock returned 50.3% from July 30 to October 28, compared with a 4.4% gain for the S&P 500. Over the past year, however, the shares returned 0.4% against 14.0% for the index, so the rally has mostly made up lost ground. What do Accenture's own results show so far?

Accenture's Sales Are Still Growing

Accenture topped its own projections in the latest quarter. Revenue for fiscal Q4 2026 reached $18.7 billion, which management said on the October 1 call was up 7% in local currency and above the top end of the guided range. The stock climbed 15.8% that day. For the full fiscal year, revenue grew 5% in local currency, and about 3% without acquisitions.

Management says building clients' data and AI foundations accounts for much of that growth. Nearly 100 additional clients started their first advanced AI projects with Accenture during the quarter, bringing the total to more than 400 in fiscal 2026.

Following the rally, the stock still trades at 17.5 times its past twelve months of earnings, compared with 22.6 for the S&P 500. Earnings expanded over the past year while the share price stagnated. Net income increased to $8.37 billion in the twelve months to August 31, from $7.68 billion a year earlier. For fiscal 2027, management expects earnings per share to grow 3% to 6% over its adjusted fiscal 2026 figure.

Can Accenture Keep Growing As Prices Slip?

Management expects growth to continue, although the company's forecast leaves room for slow growth. Prices held steady across fiscal 2026 overall. During the fourth quarter, however, management saw lower pricing in many areas of the business amid what it calls a highly competitive environment.

Accenture was already growing a little slower than the broader market. Revenue growth averaged 5.0% a year over its last three fiscal years, compared with 6.1% for the S&P 500. Management expects revenue to grow 3% to 6% in local currency for fiscal 2027, with 2% to 2.5% coming from acquisitions. At the bottom of that range, acquisitions would supply most of the growth, and management says the low end allows for clients' discretionary spending to get worse.

Management also says the loss from AI efficiencies has been steady, while new kinds of work and more scope have more than offset it.

title: Adobe vs. International Business Machines: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Adobe vs. International Business Machines: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool

Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Choosing between a creative software titan and an enterprise infrastructure legend depends on your financial goals. Deciding between Adobe (NASDAQ:ADBE) and International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) requires a close look at their growth and stability profiles.

Adobe leads the market in design and document workflows, moving aggressively into generative artificial intelligence. IBM focuses on the backbone of corporate technology, specializing in hybrid cloud and consulting. While both serve the enterprise sector, they offer distinct financial profiles, making this a choice between high-margin software and steady, global infrastructure.

The case for Adobe

Adobe develops an end-to-end platform for creative, productivity, and marketing workflows. Its solutions serve business professionals, consumers, and large enterprise marketing teams in the tech stocks market. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, the company highlighted how it integrates third-party platforms to support its content supply chain and generative AI models. It also expanded its capabilities through the acquisition of Topaz Labs L.L.C. in June 2026.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $23.8 billion, which was an increase of approximately 10.5% over the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $7.1 billion, up from approximately $5.6 billion in FY 2024. This performance led to a net margin of roughly 30%, representing the percentage of total sales remaining after all business expenses are paid. Management noted that growth was consistent across its creative and document cloud segments.

As of its November 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was nearly 0.6x, meaning for every dollar of equity held by shareholders, the company has 60 cents in total debt. The current ratio, which compares short-term assets to short-term liabilities, was approximately 1.0x. Free cash flow, defined as cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached close to $9.9 billion. This strong cash generation allows the company to reinvest in its AI-powered product roadmap.

The case for International Business Machines

International Business Machines focuses on providing hybrid cloud and AI-driven technology solutions for digital transformation. The company serves clients across a vast array of industries, including financial services, healthcare, and retail. It maintains a broad ecosystem of strategic partners, including Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW), Salesforce (NYSE:CRM), Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and SAP (NYSE:SAP). These collaborations allow the company to deliver end-to-end solutions for complex business challenges.

"Through the first nine months, we generated about $8 billion of free cash flow, up 8% year-over-year."

IBM, he said, "returned $4.8 billion to shareholders in the form of dividends through the first nine months of the year." That puts coverage near 1.7 times with the fourth quarter still ahead. Management also expects full-year free cash flow to grow by more than $1 billion.

Most of IBM's cash comes from recurring revenue. Clients pay year after year for Red Hat software, data tools, and the mainframe software that runs banks and airlines. title: IBM’s Software Business Is Picking Up Speed. Here’s Why It’s Time to Grab IBM Stock on the Dip.

IBM’s Software Business Is Picking Up Speed. Here’s Why It’s Time to Grab IBM Stock on the Dip.

International Business Machines (IBM) has spent the last couple of years trying to convince investors it's more than an old-school technology giant. A quarter ago, IBM's software story looked less comfortable, with delayed deals and timing issues clouding the outlook. The third quarter brought better news as the software business accelerated, showing strength across key areas, including Red Hat and data software.

Yet, IBM shares remain well below their $332.46 peak and are down 14% so far this year. If this momentum continues into the coming quarters, investors buying the dip could enter before the market fully recognizes the improvement in IBM's software business.

A Beaten-Down Stock Meets a Better Earnings Story

Trouble began brewing as IBM's software business lost momentum. Software revenue climbed just 5% year-over-year (YoY) in the second quarter, down sharply from 11% in the first quarter and 14% in the fourth quarter of 2025. The slowdown was upsetting because software has been central to IBM's transformation beyond its legacy hardware business. Investors had counted on this segment to drive stronger growth, so the disappointing numbers hurt confidence in the strategy. Management pointed to the company's failure to close several large software deals on schedule, leading to a delay in recognizing revenue. Yet lingering uncertainty about when that missing revenue might arrive continued to drag on the stock.

The third quarter gave a more encouraging picture. IBM generated $17.1 billion in revenue, up 5% YoY. Software revenue reached $7.8 billion, increasing 8% over the year-ago quarter and accounting for roughly 46% of total revenue. Adjusted earnings per share rose 11% to $2.95 from the year-ago quarter. During the Q3 earnings call, management stressed that software growth rose by four percentage points to reach 9% in the third quarter, backed by IBM's robust recurring-revenue base and sharper deal execution. CFO Jim Kavanaugh noted that three of four software sub-segments posted strong double-digit revenue gains, driven by a wave of new business and more effective pipeline conversion. IBM also won about two-thirds of the major deals it had missed in the second quarter. This mix of new wins and reclaimed contracts signals a rebound that goes beyond timing, pointing to deeper, more sustained momentum.
